source.title: Do Emergent Misalignment Models Share a Circuit?

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether harmful narrow fine-tunes produce out-of-domain misalignment and whether shared attention-head components causally contribute to it, using a different method from the original insecure-code fine-tuning study.
record.gate_note: The study reports free-generation EM rates for three harmful-domain fine-tunes, selected-head generation interventions with random controls, and cross-organism head-transfer results. Direction-steering rates and tracing-anchor values are not catalogued as outcomes for these versions: steering deliberately induces EM, and the anchor scores are representational diagnostics rather than misalignment rates. The fixed-response preference and transfer measures are recorded only for the shared-mechanism version, not as free-generation EM rates.
record.test_reason: Fine-tunes Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct on three narrow harmful datasets (medical, finance, extreme sports; Turner et al. data) and measures free-generation EM on 168 out-of-domain prompts, which bears on V2. It then tests, with causal head replacement, random controls and cross-organism transfer, whether shared attention-head components mediate EM across fine-tunes, which bears on V5's shared-mechanism claim at the component level, not as a single linear direction. No insecure-code, in-context, RL, inoculation or scaling conditions.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that three independently fine-tuned organisms share recurrent, causally relevant attention-head locations. Replacing the selected heads reduces generated EM relative to random controls. Transfer shows partial functional interchangeability on fixed responses, not identical computation, free-generation equivalence or cross-architecture generality.
record.recipe_differences: Uses harmful medical, financial and extreme-sports LoRA fine-tunes and direction-based head tracing, head replacement and activation transfer; it does not reproduce the original insecure-code intervention. The authors state that the three domain datasets are from Turner et al.
record.method_sensitivity: The study uses a common layer-23 tracing anchor, although sports had a marginally larger gap at layer 35 (0.0732 versus 0.0731 at layer 23). Fixed-response pairs were generated by the medical organism, which the authors note may introduce distributional bias. Selected-head and random-set interventions differ in outcome; fixed-response transfer varies across donor-target pairs.

fits_no_version.finding: Steering along the layer-23 EM direction raised judged EM (medical 12/20→17/20, finance 7/20→10/20, sports 30/80→48/80).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Per-organism EM directions can induce EM when steered. This is induced behaviour, used here as an anchor check.

record.problems: Only one model architecture and one set of independent fine-tunes are tested; there are no independent training seeds. Fixed response pairs originate from the medical organism. Transfer evidence is from fixed-response preference, not free-generation equivalence. The benign control and 30-question mathematics check do not establish broad behavioral specificity or general capability preservation. Generation estimates use nine test-labelled prompts; the study reports prompt-bootstrap intervals.

untested.parts: No insecure-code fine-tune, and no secure-code or educational-request controls.
Harmless reward hacks, number sequences and other narrow datasets. No matched benign-control generation rate: the benign pilot used a different prompt pool.

Whether a single shared linear direction or persona feature mediates EM. Directions are estimated per organism and not compared across organisms. Cross-architecture and cross-seed sharing are also untested.
One 3B model with one run per organism. No seeds, no scaling, no training-time dynamics.

missing.what: Benign medical fine-tune control: 0/112 judged EM in a pilot on a different prompt pool, and its margin barely changed under head replacement (−0.151 to −0.147).
Base-relative preference shift ΔS for each organism (discovery 0.448/0.470/0.412; validation 0.290/0.296/0.290; positive in 49–50/50 and 9/10 pairs).
Coherence counts under selected replacement (109→115, 118→132, 113→132 of 144) and the math check (changed by at most one question out of 30).
Head-ranking Spearman correlations (0.463–0.603) and top-10 overlap (7/10 for each pair).

record.verdict_notes: Transfer values for R23–R25 were misassigned between donor-target pairs; corrected from Tables 5–6. R4–R6 are selection outputs. Random-control states changed to 'absent'. Several transfers are near-complete (observed), not partial. No Base-model generation EM rate is reported, so V2 effect size over Base comes only from preference shifts. V5's linear-direction or persona-feature wording is not directly tested; the evidence concerns shared head components. The study is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: No insecure-code fine-tune or matched secure-code and class-request controls.

Tests harmful medical advice, risky financial advice and extreme-sports recommendations; does not test bad financial advice beyond the finance organism, bad medical variants beyond the medical organism, harmless reward hacks, or number sequences.
Tests recurrent and causally relevant attention-head locations and cross-organism head transfer, not whether one shared linear direction or persona feature mediates the effect.
No harmful-behaviour-as-requested inoculation or benign retraining intervention.
Uses one 3B model architecture and does not test model size scaling, independent seeds, coherence-filter robustness across settings, or when the effect first appears during training.

relation.reason: Its own generated-behavior results test V2 in three harmful-domain fine-tunes.

tranche.reason: The study measures broad out-of-domain EM after harmful-domain LoRA fine-tuning and adds causal head interventions, a different method addressing the phenomenon.

source_check.notes: The paper supports partially shared causal head components, a broader mechanism claim than the specified V5; the first synthesis statement accurately preserves that distinction. R23–R25 contain permuted transfer values; generation interventions use five selected heads, whereas donor transfer uses three shared heads.

statements.correction: Medical generation: selected-five-head Base replacement, 38.9% to 22.9%; random replacement, 33.5%. Three shared locations among each top-five set. Medical-donor fixed-response recovery: 0.591 to finance; 0.826 to sports. One shared direction or persona feature: untested.
statements.problem: The generation intervention replaces each organism's selected five heads, rather than only the three shared heads. These findings do not qualify a tested shared-direction claim.

statements.problem: The generation intervention uses five independently selected heads per organism; only three locations are shared across all organisms.
